name: White button mushroom extract
lead: White button mushroom (Agaricus bisporus) is the common cultivated mushroom, grown in more than 70 countries; its brown form is sold as cremini and the mature form as portobello.[1] In bodybuilding and hormone-optimisation circles its extract is discussed as a food-derived aromatase inhibitor, a substance that might reduce the conversion of androgens into estrogens.[2][6]

People interested in physique use the idea as follows: estrogen control is associated with a leaner, drier look, less breast tissue and less estrogen-related water retention, so a mild natural aromatase inhibitor is attractive to some men on testosterone therapy or training for aesthetics. Posts on T Nation ask whether white button mushroom or its extract can lower estradiol without a prescription aromatase inhibitor such as anastrozole.[8][9]

Wikipedia's aromatase inhibitor page reports that mushroom extracts inhibited aromatase in enzyme assays, white mushroom most strongly, and cites a 2009 case-control study of 2,018 women in southeast China linking higher mushroom intake to lower breast cancer incidence, which it describes as small and regional.[2] Registered human trials of the extract concern breast and prostate cancer rather than appearance.

chain: Extract compounds reported to inhibit aromatase in lab assays
Possible lower estrogen conversion from testosterone
Claimed leaner, less puffy look and less breast-tissue tendency
angle.text: Users add the mushroom or extract to diets and supplement stacks hoping to modestly lower estrogen. The proposed link between estrogen and looks is water retention, body-fat distribution and gynecomastia; human data on whether the extract changes these are limited to cancer-focused trials.

paras: Raw white mushrooms provide about 22 kcal per 100 g and are a source of riboflavin, niacin and pantothenic acid; UV exposure raises vitamin D2 content.[1] The species is a model fungus whose genome has been sequenced.[3] The mushroom also contains tyrosinase, a copper enzyme involved in browning, whose crystal structure has been described.[10]
Nutrient surveys of cultivated mushrooms report vitamins, minerals and phenolic compounds in white button mushrooms.[11]

Aromatase is the enzyme that converts androgens to estrogens. Prescription inhibitors such as anastrozole and letrozole block it and are used mainly in hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer, with other uses including gynecomastia in some settings and estrogen management during testosterone therapy.[2]

In enzyme assays described by Wikipedia, mushroom extracts reduced aromatase activity, white mushroom most strongly.[2] The page notes this is laboratory evidence and that the population study linking mushroom intake to breast cancer incidence was limited in scope.[2] A review of edible mushrooms in breast cancer covers Agaricus bisporus among species studied for anticancer effects, including dietary intake studies and clinical work on extracts.[17] T Nation posters note it is uncertain whether eating mushrooms has the same effect as an extract.[9]

On T Nation, a 2018 thread on reducing 'estrogen bodyfat' during testosterone replacement asks about natural aromatase inhibitors and mentions Agaricus bisporus extract.[8] A 2014 thread on high estradiol includes a user who read that white button mushrooms may reduce estradiol and asks whether anyone has tried them.[9] Older multi-ingredient bodybuilding supplements have listed Agaricus bisporus alongside other 'pro-androgen' ingredients.[12][13]
These posts show interest rather than reported outcomes; replies in the sources describe the question as open.

sections.h: Other human research on the food
paras: A randomized crossover study of 32 healthy adults compared protein-matched servings of A. bisporus mushrooms and meat for ten days and measured satiety and food intake.[14] Separate studies have looked at gut health markers, and a 2024 trial found that adding mushrooms to a Mediterranean-style pattern did not change most short-term cardiometabolic risk factors.[15][16] None of these measured estrogen or appearance.

As a common food it is widely eaten. Concentrated-extract safety data were not reviewed here. Wild lookalikes such as the death cap are dangerous, but that concerns foraging rather than cultivated products.

Registered studies on ClinicalTrials.gov include a Phase I trial of white button mushroom extract in postmenopausal breast cancer survivors (16 participants, started 2008, completed),[4] a Phase I trial in men with recurrent prostate cancer after local therapy (36 participants, started 2009, completed),[5] a trial on inflammation in obese postmenopausal women at high risk of breast cancer (26 participants, started 2021),[6] and a Phase II trial on PSA in prostate cancer (133 planned participants, suspended).[7] These registrations concern cancer-related outcomes, not appearance. No studies of white button mushroom extract for appearance or bodybuilding goals were found.

timeline.event: Phase I trial of white button mushroom extract in breast cancer survivors begins.[4]
Phase I prostate cancer trial starts; a Chinese case-control study links mushroom intake to lower breast cancer incidence.[5][2]
New registered trials on inflammation and PSA begin.[6]

lore.intro: Within supplement and TRT discussion, white button mushroom is brought up as a food-based option for estrogen control.[8][9]

claims.claim: White button mushroom extract works as a natural aromatase inhibitor
claims.believers: Users have read that mushroom extract lowers estradiol and ask for personal experience as an alternative to prescription inhibitors.[8][9]
claims.experts: Enzyme assays reported aromatase inhibition; human trials registered so far address cancer outcomes and no trial of estradiol in men for appearance was found.[2][4]

claims.claim: Eating the whole mushroom is as effective as the extract
claims.believers: Some users suggest dietary button mushrooms may help reduce estradiol.[9]
claims.experts: Forum replies note uncertainty about food versus extract, and the assay data concern extracts.[2][9]

claims.claim: Lower estrogen gives a leaner, less puffy physique
claims.believers: Posters link estradiol to bodyfat and water retention in testosterone therapy.[8]
claims.experts: Aromatase inhibitors are used clinically to manage estrogen, with documented side effects such as joint problems and bone effects.[2]

card.summary: A common food whose extracts inhibit aromatase in lab assays; human work is cancer-focused and not about looks.
card.note: Lab assay findings; no appearance outcomes tested in humans.

quick.overview:
White button mushroom is an everyday food. Extracts have been reported to inhibit aromatase in enzyme assays, which is why it appears in lists of natural aromatase inhibitors.

Human trials found were registered for cancer-related questions; none addressed appearance.
quick.mechanism: Compounds in the mushroom are reported to reduce aromatase enzyme activity in vitro.
quick.risks: As a common food it is widely eaten; safety data for concentrated extracts were not reviewed in depth. Wild lookalikes such as the death cap are dangerous, but that concerns foraging, not the cultivated product.
